I verified this by running each one's tests in a temp copy and by probing edge cases: bad ids, a corrupt file with each command, the default file, tmp files, prototype-key commands, and huge or negative ids. So the ranking rests on code quality, tests, robustness and docs.

Its real weakness is robustness on valid JSON with the wrong shape: a null entry in todos crashes with a stack trace. That case is outside the spec's 'not valid JSON' rule, so it costs less than the gaps in the other two.

Its tests are well organised and clean up after themselves, but they never test the shape validation the code does, and they miss some id edge cases. Its README is accurate but thinner.

3. Y ranks last. It is the most robust on unexpected I/O errors (a friendly message instead of a stack trace) and validates shape deeply. The user sees a raw Node stack trace that leaks absolute paths. Z.notes: All 28 of its own tests pass, and every spec line is met. The url goes straight into writeHead, which throws ERR_INVALID_CHAR (app.mjs:125-127). The same happens for URLs with an embedded \n, which isHttpUrl accepts because the WHATWG parser strips the character (app.mjs:71-78). The core redirect therefore breaks for a class of valid inputs, and no test covers it.
- HEAD / returns 404 (not required by the spec).
- code:null is treated as absent: lenient but documented.

X.notes: Own suite: 34/34 pass, about 95% line coverage. My black-box probe (around 75 checks run against `node server.mjs`) failed 2 of them, both from the same cause. DEFECT: server.mjs:70 always sends `Location: new URL(url).href`, so the stored URL is normalised rather than sent as stored. `https://example.com` redirects to `https://example.com/`, and `https://Example.COM/Path?x=1#frag` loses its host case. The spec says Location is the stored url, and a plain create-then-redirect equality test on `https://example.com` fails. The README ("302 with Location: <url>") does not mention this. Everything else matched the spec. Check order is 429, 415, 413, 400, 409 (server.mjs:38-49). It rejects whitespace and control characters before URL.canParse (server.mjs:20), compares the admin token in constant time with hashing (server.mjs:29-34), and inserts atomically, catching only the PK-violation errcodes (store.mjs:45-63). Static files are guarded against traversal, including malformed %-escapes (static.mjs:18-29). A 413 response sets Connection: close (server.mjs:97). The rate limiter has bounded memory, prunes idle keys and has its own unit tests (rate-limit.mjs). createApp lets tests inject now, rateLimit and publicDir, and the module layout is clean (server/store/rate-limit/static/http-utils). Tests cover the exact 10240-byte boundary, a streamed 413 without Content-Length, rolling-window recovery with an injected clock, 429 before 415, raw-socket traversal paths, non-ASCII redirects and a spawned `listening on` check. The api.js fetch tests cover network errors, non-JSON error bodies and non-JSON 2xx. The frontend is polished (aria-live, busy state, copy button, href only for http(s)) and verified working in a browser. Minor gap: app.js DOM wiring is untested beyond a grep for innerHTML.

Y.notes: Own suite: 84/84 pass, about 96% line coverage. My probe failed 3 checks, plus behaviour I logged as INFO. DEFECTS: (1) validateUrl (server.mjs:106-119) relies only on `new URL`, so it accepts `http:/a.com` and `http:example.com`, which are not absolute http:// URLs. It also accepts `https://a.com/a b` and `'  https://a.com/ws  '` and stores them verbatim with the whitespace. (2) validateCode (server.mjs:122) treats `code: ''` and `null` as absent and returns 201 with a random code. The spec says an invalid code must be 400; this is documented in the README but still deviates. (3) Every JSON response has `Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8` (server.mjs:72), not the bare `application/json` the spec names, so a strict equality check fails. (4) When more than 10k IPs are tracked, the rate limiter wipes all state (server.mjs:57-61), so an attacker with many addresses (IPv6) can reset everyone's limit. This is acknowledged in a comment. (5) PORT is not validated (server.mjs:289). (6) createApp does not expose the clock, so rolling-window recovery is never tested. STRENGTHS: Location is sent verbatim, falling back to the encoded href only for non-header-safe characters (server.mjs:216). Token comparison is timing-safe. A 413 sets Connection: close. Static serving is traversal-safe and sends nosniff. The check order is correct. Tests are well split by area and include raw traversal paths, a spoofed X-Forwarded-For, the 10240 boundary, a chunked 413, 429 before 415, both empty and unset ADMIN_TOKEN, and a spawned server. The api.js tests are thorough, with an injected fetch, network failures and empty or invalid bodies. The README is the best of the three, with a PowerShell example, status tables and createApp usage. The whole server is one 292-line file: tidy, but less modular than the others. The frontend works in a browser and uses only textContent.

Z.notes: Own suite: 54/54 pass, about 97.5% line coverage, and the frontend app.js reaches 100%. My probe found 0 failures. The redirect keeps Location verbatim and encodes only non-header-safe URLs (app.mjs:91). URL validation is strict: it requires an http(s):// prefix, rejects whitespace and control characters, and requires a non-empty hostname (app.mjs:18-27). `code: ''` gets 400. The check order is 429, 415, 413, 400, 409 (app.mjs:63-69, http.mjs:31-47). Rejected POSTs count toward the limit, and X-Forwarded-For is ignored. The store uses INSERT OR IGNORE and checks `changes`, which avoids sniffing errcodes (store.mjs:28-44). Every response sends nosniff, and HTML also gets a CSP (http.mjs:11,104,129). The rate-limit sweeper is unref'd and cleared on close, the server shuts down cleanly on SIGINT/SIGTERM (server.mjs:18-23), PORT is validated, and Windows-specific fs errors (EINVAL, ENAMETOOLONG) map to 404 (http.mjs:121). The structure is clean (server/app/http/store), with createApp accepting rateLimit and now. Minor cohesion issue: the rate limiter lives in http.mjs. Frontend tests stand out: they drive the exported fetch, render and init functions through a FakeElement whose innerHTML throws. That checks textContent and form wiring for real, not only with a grep. A spawned-server test checks PORT, DB_FILE, ADMIN_TOKEN and persistence across a restart. WEAKNESSES: the traversal tests use fetch (api.test.mjs:236), and WHATWG normalises `%2e%2e`, so that case is not really exercised. There is no test at the exact 10240-byte boundary and none for 429 before 415. server.test.mjs picks a random fixed port rather than PORT=0, a small flake risk. A 413 drains the rest of the body rather than closing the connection (http.mjs:37-40, 57-60). The frontend fetch logic has no friendly network-error message or empty-input guard, there is no busy state, and createdAt is shown as raw ISO. GET or PUT on /api/links returns 404 instead of 405, which the spec allows. The README is concise, accurate and includes a coverage script.

reasoning: I read all three in full, ran each suite in a temp copy (all green) and ran the same black-box spec probe against `node server.mjs` for each. I also smoke-tested every frontend in a browser: all three create links and look up stats, render `<b>` as text, and show the 409 message. Z ranks first because it was the only one with no spec deviation anywhere in the probe. It has strict URL and code validation, a verbatim Location header, the correct check order and correct DELETE and auth semantics, solid security headers, and the only tests that exercise the frontend's DOM rendering and wiring. Its weaker spots are some test gaps (fetch-normalised traversal paths, no 10240-byte boundary test) and a plainer frontend. X is the most polished on engineering: modular code, injectable clock, very good tests and careful hardening. But it rewrites every redirect target through `new URL().href`, so `https://example.com` redirects to `https://example.com/` and host case is lost. That breaks the spec's \"Location set to the stored url\" in the most common case. Y gets the redirect right but has several smaller spec deviations. It accepts non-absolute or whitespace-padded URLs such as `http:/a.com` and `'  https://...  '`, treats `code: ''` as no code instead of 400, and appends charset to the JSON Content-Type. Its rate limiter can be reset by a many-IP flood, and its 292-line single file is less modular. Its tests are broad but cannot check rolling-window recovery. X's single defect plus its stronger tests and structure put it above Y's cluster of leniencies.

X.notes: npm test: 34/34 pass (coverage about 95% lines). My black-box probe (node server.mjs with PORT, DB_FILE and ADMIN_TOKEN) passed every check except one. Strengths: modules are cleanly split (src/store.mjs, rate-limit.mjs, static.mjs, http-utils.mjs). URL validation is strict (server.mjs:16-22: needs a literal http(s):// prefix, rejects whitespace and control characters, then URL.canParse). Rate limit is checked before the 415 check. The admin token is compared with a SHA-256 hash and timingSafeEqual. Invalid PORT values are rejected (server.mjs:129). 413 responses send Connection: close. The rate limiter takes an injectable clock and prunes stale entries once per window. Tests cover rolling-window recovery and a flooding key (tests 6 and 19), and path traversal against a fixture publicDir with a secret file outside it (test 12). Defects: (1) server.mjs:70 always sends Location as new URL(url).href, so the redirect does not use the stored URL. Posting https://a.com redirects to https://a.com/, and https://Example.com:443/a/../b redirects to https://example.com/b. The spec says Location is the stored url, and the README (line 69) claims the same. A plain-domain grader test would fail. (2) The spawn test (test 14) only checks the listening line with PORT=0. It does not check that DB_FILE is used, the default port, or the short link. (3) public/app.js (DOM rendering) has no tests; only api.js and a grep for innerHTML are covered. (4) Error handling mixes two styles: some paths throw HttpError and others return sendError. (5) No graceful shutdown and no CSP. Strengths: one cohesive 292-line server.mjs. Rate limit is checked before the 415 check. Body size is enforced both by Content-Length and while streaming, with Connection: close on 413. The admin token is compared with timingSafeEqual over hashes. 405 is returned for a wrong method on a known route. The many tests include the exact 10240-byte boundary, a chunked 413, a spoofed X-Forwarded-For, case-sensitive codes, a 9-path traversal suite with raw requests, an unset or empty ADMIN_TOKEN, and spawning server.mjs. public/api.js is thoroughly tested and never rejects. The README is the most detailed of the three, with per-endpoint status tables and a programmatic createApp example. Defects: (1) validateCode (server.mjs:122) treats code:"" and code:null as absent and generates a random code (201). The spec says a provided code that does not match the pattern gets 400. (2) validateUrl uses only new URL plus a protocol check. It accepts 'http:/a.com' and ' https://ws.com' (leading space, stored raw), which are not literally absolute http:// URLs. (3) JSON responses use 'application/json; charset=utf-8' rather than exactly application/json, so a strict equality check would fail. (4) PORT is not validated: PORT=abc makes listen throw. (5) The rate limiter (server.mjs:57-61) wipes every client's counters when more than 10k IPs are tracked, so a distributed flood resets everyone's limit. Z.notes: npm test: 54/54 pass (coverage about 97.5% lines). The black-box probe passed every check: listening line, DB file created, 201/409/400/415/413/429, the 21st POST blocked, stats with ISO createdAt, 302 with the exact stored Location, clicks incremented, DELETE returning 401/404/204, static content types, and traversal attempts (raw, %2f, %5c, malformed encoding) all 404. Strengths: clear split into src/app.mjs (routing), src/store.mjs (INSERT OR IGNORE, so creation is atomic with no race) and src/http.mjs. URL validation is strict (app.mjs:18-27: literal prefix, no whitespace or control characters, URL parse, non-empty host). A provided code that is empty or null gets 400, as the spec says. Location is the stored url unless it is not header-safe (app.mjs:91). The admin token is compared with timingSafeEqual over hashes. The rate limiter has an injected clock, memory bounded by slice, and a periodic unref'd sweep. index.html is served with a CSP and nosniff. PORT is validated. SIGINT/SIGTERM shut down gracefully. Tests stand out: a fake DOM whose innerHTML getter and setter throw proves rendering uses textContent; init() form wiring is tested; rolling-window reset is tested with a fake clock; and a spawn test checks PORT, DB_FILE, ADMIN_TOKEN, the short link and persistence across a restart. Minor: no 405 for wrong methods (returns 404). After an oversized body it drains the rest instead of closing the connection. The form button is not disabled while a request is pending. src/http.mjs is a bit of a grab-bag (body reading, limiter and static files). The README is accurate and concise, notes the X-Forwarded-For caveat and gives PowerShell and sh examples, but is less detailed than Y's.

reasoning: Z did not deviate from the spec anywhere I probed. It also has the strongest tests: they check that DOM rendering never uses innerHTML (the fake innerHTML throws), test the form wiring through init(), test the rolling window with an injected clock, and spawn server.mjs to check persistence and every env setting. Its hardening is the best of the three (CSP, graceful shutdown, PORT validation). Y is solid, documented in the most detail and has the largest test suite. Its gaps are interpretive leniencies rather than broken behaviour: an empty or null code gets a random code instead of 400, URL validation is looser, and JSON responses carry a charset parameter. It also has a weaker rate limiter that wipes all counters under a large flood, no PORT validation, and no rolling-window recovery test. X is well structured and has good limiter and traversal tests. However, it has a confirmed defect in a core path: every redirect's Location is normalized with new URL(url).href instead of using the stored url. https://a.com becomes https://a.com/, and the host case, default port and dot segments are changed. This contradicts both the spec and X's own README, and a typical grader test would catch it. Its spawn and DOM test coverage is also thinner than Y's, so X ranks last.
